name: Doppler echo cardiac output
seoDesc: Doppler echo cardiac output: work out body surface area from the height and the weight. A free health calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: body surface area is what the Doppler echo cardiac output calculator works out, and it gets there from the height, the weight, the heart rate and the LVOT diameter. Think of it as a shortcut for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. Change one value and the results step aside until you press Calculate again, which is what makes it easy to see how much the answer really depends on that one input.

sections.title: How does the Doppler echo cardiac output calculator work?
sections.html:
The Doppler echo cardiac output calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports body surface area in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the height, the weight, the heart rate and the LVOT diameter.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Doppler echo cardiac output calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Body surface area=(1 ÷ 60) × the square root of (height × weight)
Cross sectional area of LVOT=(1 ÷ 4) × PI × (LVOT diameter ^ 2)
LVOT VTI=stroke volume ÷ cross sectional area of LVOT
Cardiac output=(1 ÷ 1000) × stroke volume × heart rate
Cardiac output=(1 ÷ 60) × cardiac index × the square root of (height × weight)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in square meters, and convertible to any of the 24 units on that chip.
  • Shown in square centimeters, and convertible to any of the 24 units on that chip.
  • Shown in centimeters, and convertible to any of the 34 units on that chip.
  • Shown in minutes, and convertible to any of the 27 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Time, opening in minutes
  • Volume, opening in milliliters
  • Area, opening in square centimeters
  • Area, opening in square meters

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Doppler echo cardiac output calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the height, the weight and the heart rate — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Doppler echo cardiac output calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns body surface area, derived from the height, the weight and the heart rate. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Doppler echo cardiac output calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the height, the weight, the heart rate and the LVOT diameter, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter height in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Height opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: Is the Doppler echo cardiac output calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
